claim: CAD cells are derived from a mouse brain tumor and can be induced by serum starvation to display features of neuronal differentiation, including cell cycle downregulation, expression of neuronal markers, and the appearance of neuronal morphologies.
source: CAD cells are derived from a mouse brain tumor and can be induced by serum starvation to display features of neuronal differentiation, including cell cycle downregulation, expression of neuronal markers, and the appearance of neuronal morphologies (Qi et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Qi et al., 1997, which provides external evidence for the properties of CAD cells.

claim: The CAD FMRP knockout line has a single basepair deletion in all alleles of Fmr1.
source: The CAD FMRP knockout line was found to have a single basepair deletion in all alleles of Fmr1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1, which displays Sanger sequencing tracks confirming the deletion.

claim: The single basepair deletion in the CAD FMRP knockout line caused a frameshift and a premature termination codon two codons downstream of the gRNA cut site.
source: The CAD FMRP knockout line was found to have a single basepair deletion in all alleles of Fmr1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) that caused a frameshift and a premature termination codon two codons downstream of the gRNA cut site.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observed single basepair deletion and knowledge of how such mutations affect reading frames.

claim: The premature termination codon in the CAD FMRP knockout line was upstream of all identified RNA-binding domains in FMRP.
source: The premature termination codon was upstream of all identified RNA-binding domains in FMRP.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the location of the premature stop codon and knowledge of FMRP domain structure.

claim: The CAD FMRP knockout cells displayed no detectable FMRP expression by immunoblotting, even when probed with a polyclonal FMRP antibody.
source: The knockout cells displayed no detectable FMRP expression by immunoblotting, even when probed with a polyclonal FMRP antibody (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B, which shows a Western blot comparing wildtype and knockout cells.

claim: 86 genes displayed impaired neurite localization in the FMR1 knockout cells compared to wildtype cells.
source: Using Xtail and a false discovery rate cutoff of 0.01, we identified 86 genes whose transcripts displayed impaired neurite localization, and thus decreased LR values, in the FMR1 knockout (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 10, Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis using Xtail software and is shown in Figure 1D and supplementary materials.

claim: FMRP localization targets are enriched for genes that regulate vesicle transport in neurons.
source: Gene ontology analysis of these targets revealed that they were enriched for genes that regulate vesicle transport in neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 11).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 11.

claim: mRNAs encoding several kinesins were less localized in the FMRP knockout.
source: In particular, mRNAs encoding several kinesins were less localized in the FMRP knockout.
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis of mislocalized transcripts in the FMRP knockout.

claim: mRNAs encoding kinesins have been recently identified as both bound and transported by FMRP in glial cells.
source: Interestingly, mRNAs encoding kinesins have been recently identified as both bound and transported by FMRP in glial cells (Pilaz et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pilaz et al., 2016.

claim: The expression of FMRP localization targets did not change in the soma between wildtype and FMRP knockout samples.
source: We found that while the expression of FMRP localization targets did not change in the soma between the wildtype and FMRP knockout samples, their expression in the neurites of FMRP knockout cells was significantly reduced (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by expression data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The expression of FMRP localization targets in the neurites of FMRP knockout cells was significantly reduced compared to wildtype.
source: We found that while the expression of FMRP localization targets did not change in the soma between the wildtype and FMRP knockout samples, their expression in the neurites of FMRP knockout cells was significantly reduced (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by expression data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: FMRP localization targets were approximately 4-fold more likely to be directly bound by FMRP than expected by chance.
source: FMRP localization targets were approximately 4-fold more likely to be directly bound by FMRP than expected by chance (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of CLIP-seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: FMRP CLIP-seq targets were preferentially mislocalized in FMRP knockout cells compared to CLIP-seq nontargets.
source: We then performed the converse analysis to ask whether FMRP CLIP-seq targets were preferentially mislocalized in FMRP knockout cells. We found that the localization of FMRP CLIP-seq targets was significantly more sensitive to FMRP loss than CLIP-seq nontargets (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The RNA sequence 'GGA' was strongly enriched in the 3′ UTR of FMRP localization targets.
source: We observed a strong enrichment for the RNA sequence 'GGA' in the 3′ UTR of FMRP localization targets (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by 6mer enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: GGA had previously been identified from an FMRP CLIP-seq dataset as a preferred FMRP binding motif.
source: GGA had previously been identified from an FMRP CLIP-seq dataset as a preferred FMRP binding motif, giving us further confidence that our identified localization targets were directly bound and regulated by FMRP (Ascano et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ascano et al., 2012.

claim: Tandem repeats of GGA sequences are known to have the ability to fold into G-quadruplex sequences.
source: Tandem repeats of GGA sequences are known to have the ability to fold into G-quadruplex sequences (Suhl et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Suhl et al., 2014 and represents established knowledge.

claim: G-quadruplex structures have been shown to be specifically bound by FMRP in vitro.
source: Given that G-quadruplex structures have been shown to be specifically bound by FMRP in vitro, (Didiot et al., 2008; Vasilyev et al., 2015), we then asked if G-quadruplex sequences were enriched in FMRP localization target sequences.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Didiot et al., 2008 and Vasilyev et al., 2015.

claim: The 3′ UTRs of FMRP localization targets contained significantly more G-quadruplex sequences than nontargets, as determined by both a regular expression method and RNAfold.
source: Both methods agreed that the 3′ UTRs of FMRP localization targets contained significantly more G-quadruplex sequences than nontargets (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis data shown in Figures 2D and 2E.

claim: Experimentally defined G-quadruplexes were significantly enriched in the 3′ UTRs of FMRP localization targets.
source: As with the computational predictions, we observed a significant enrichment of experimentally defined G-quadruplexes in the 3′ UTRs of FMRP localization targets (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis using experimentally defined G-quadruplex data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: FMRP localization targets had much longer open reading frames and 3′ UTRs than expected.
source: We observed that FMRP localization targets had much longer open reading frames and 3′ UTRs than expected (Figure 2G)
evidence: This claim is supported by transcript feature analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: 3′ UTR extensions and alternative 3′ UTRs can regulate RNA localization in neurons.
source: We observed that FMRP localization targets had much longer open reading frames and 3′ UTRs than expected (Figure 2G), consistent with previous reports that 3′ UTR extensions and alternative 3′ UTRs can regulate RNA localization in neurons (Taliaferro et al., 2016a; Tushev et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Taliaferro et al., 2016a and Tushev et al., 2018.

claim: There was no relationship between the overall abundance of a transcript and whether or not it was an FMRP localization target.
source: We observed no relationship between the overall abundance of a transcript and whether or not it was an FMRP localization target.
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis of transcript features.

claim: The enrichment of G-quadruplexes in FMRP localization targets was restricted to their 3′ UTRs.
source: The enrichment of G-quadruplexes in FMRP localization targets was restricted to their 3′ UTRs as we did not observe a significant relationship between CDS or 5′ UTR G-quadruplex density and localization regulation by FMRP (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by transcript feature analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Guanosines in quadruplexes were less conserved than those not in quadruplexes.
source: Surprisingly, we found that guanosines in quadruplexes were less conserved than those not in quadruplexes, and those in FMRP localization targets were less conserved than those in nontargets (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by PhyloP conservation analysis shown in Figure 2H.

claim: There was a significant enrichment of G-quadruplexes in the human orthologs of the FMRP localization targets.
source: We observed a significant enrichment of G-quadruplexes in the human orthologs of the FMRP localization targets, arguing that their function may be conserved across species (Figure 2I,J).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of human ortholog sequences shown in Figures 2I and 2J.

claim: The FXS neurons displayed a large decrease in both FMR1 RNA and FMRP protein.
source: As expected, the FXS neurons displayed a large decrease in both FMR1 RNA and FMRP protein (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: The human orthologs of the mouse FMRP localization targets were significantly less neurite-localized in FXS neurons than in unaffected neurons.
source: Strikingly, the human orthologs of the mouse FMRP localization targets were significantly less neurite-localized in FXS neurons than in unaffected neurons, indicating that the functional localization targets of FMRP were broadly conserved across species (mouse and human) and experimental systems (neuronal cell line and iPS-derived neurons) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by localization data from iPS-derived neurons shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There was a modest but highly significant correlation between the mislocalization of genes in the CAD knockout system and the mislocalization of their human orthologs in the FXS iPS system.
source: Overall, we observed a modest (R = 0.21) but highly significant (p=1e-37) correlation between the mislocalization of genes in the CAD knockout system and the mislocalization of their human orthologs in the FXS iPS system (Figure 3—figure supplement 5, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: FMRP targets in human iPS-derived neurons were significantly more likely to be directly bound by FMRP in cells than FMRP nontargets.
source: We found that FMRP targets were significantly more likely to be directly bound by FMRP in cells as determined by CLIP than FMRP nontargets (Figure 3D; Ascano et al., 2012; Darnell et al., 2011; Maurin et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by CLIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: FMRP targets in human iPS-derived neurons had significantly higher densities of G-quadruplexes in their 3′ UTRs than FMRP nontargets.
source: We also found that FMRP targets had significantly higher densities of G-quadruplexes in their 3′ UTRs than FMRP nontargets, suggesting that this mode of localization target recognition may be conserved between mice and humans (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by G-quadruplex density analysis shown in Figures 3E and 3F.

claim: G-quadruplex RNA sequences were approximately 10-fold enriched in the RGG-associated RNA compared to the input pool in RBNS experiments.
source: G-quadruplex RNA sequences, defined either as matches to specific motifs or through RNA folding predictions, were approximately 10-fold enriched in the RGG-associated RNA compared to the input pool (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RBNS experimental data shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: The addition of lithium drastically reduced the enrichment of G-quadruplex sequences in RGG-associated RNA.
source: Furthermore, the addition of lithium drastically reduced this enrichment of G-quadruplex sequences, indicating that the G-quadruplexes must be folded in order to interact with the RGG domain in vitro, as has been previously observed (Menon et al., 2008; Ramos et al., 2003; Schaeffer et al., 2001; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by RBNS experimental data and citations to previous studies.

claim: The RGG domain interacted with a G-quadruplex RNA in the presence of potassium with a high affinity (Kd ~30 nM).
source: Using fluorescence polarization assays, we found that the RGG domain interacted with a G-quadruplex RNA in the presence of potassium with a high affinity (Kd ~30 nM).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence polarization assay data.

claim: The KH domains of FMRP did not specifically interact with G-quadruplex sequences.
source: The KH domains of FMRP did not specifically interact with G-quadruplex sequences (Figure 4C,D)
evidence: This claim is supported by RBNS experimental data shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: The reporter transcript containing the Nol3 3′ UTR with a G-quadruplex sequence was efficiently localized to neurites, but only in cells expressing full length FMRP.
source: We observed that the reporter transcript that contained a G-quadruplex sequence in its 3′ UTR was efficiently localized to neurites, but only in cells expressing full length FMRP (FMRP, Nol3 3′ UTR), and not in cells either completely lacking FMRP (GFP, Nol3 3′ UTR) or in cells expressing only a truncated form of FMRP (ΔRGG, Nol3 3′ UTR) (Figure 5C,D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by smFISH experimental data shown in Figures 5C, 5D, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Removal of the G-quadruplex sequence from the reporter transcript resulted in less efficient transcript localization regardless of the FMRP status of the cell.
source: Removal of the G-quadruplex sequence (Nol3-G4 3′ UTR) resulted in less efficient transcript localization regardless of the FMRP status of the cell (Figure 5C,D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by smFISH experimental data shown in Figures 5C, 5D, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ΔRGG truncation showed significantly reduced interaction with the G-quadruplex-containing Firefly reporter compared to full length FMRP.
source: We found that the ΔRGG truncation showed significantly reduced interaction with the G-quadruplex-containing Firefly reporter compared to full length FMRP (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by CLIP-qPCR experimental data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Both full length FMRP and the ΔRGG truncation showed reduced, but equal, ability to bind the Firefly reporter lacking the G-quadruplex.
source: When we repeated the experiment using the Firefly reporter lacking the G-quadruplex, both full length FMRP and the ΔRGG truncation showed reduced, but importantly, equal, ability to bind the transcript (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by CLIP-qPCR experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Cells expressing full length FMRP and the ΔRGG truncation displayed approximately equal proportions of the total cellular FMRP in their neurites.
source: We found that cells expressing full length FMRP and the ΔRGG truncation displayed approximately equal proportions of the total cellular FMRP in their neurites, indicating that the full length protein and the truncation are trafficked to neurites at approximately similar levels (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Genes that were significantly more localized in the FMRP rescue cells contained significantly more G-quadruplex sequences in their 3′ UTRs than expected when comparing GFP rescue samples to full length FMRP rescue samples.
source: When we compared the GFP rescue samples and full length FMRP rescue samples, we found that genes that were significantly more localized in the FMRP rescue cells contained significantly more G-quadruplex sequences in their 3′ UTRs than expected, consistent with our previous results (Figures 6B and 2D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptome-wide sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Genes whose localization was significantly more efficient in the full length FMRP samples contained significantly more 3′ UTR G-quadruplex sequences than expected when comparing FMRPΔRGG rescue samples to full length FMRP rescue samples.
source: When we performed the same analysis comparing the FMRPΔRGG rescue samples to the full length FMRP rescue samples, we again found that genes whose localization was significantly more efficient in the full length FMRP samples contained significantly more 3′ UTR G-quadruplex sequences than expected (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptome-wide sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: There was no relationship between the G-quadruplex content of an RNA and its differential localization in the GFP rescue and FMRPΔRGG rescue samples.
source: Consistent with this, we observed no relationship between the G-quadruplex content of an RNA and its differential localization in the GFP rescue and FMRPΔRGG rescue samples (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Genes that displayed reduced ribosome occupancy in FMRP null cells compared to wildtype cells were significantly more likely to have been identified as FMRP CLIP targets than expected.
source: We found genes that displayed reduced ribosome occupancy in FMRP null cells compared to wildtype cells were significantly more likely to have been identified as FMRP CLIP targets than expected (Figure 7B; Ascano et al., 2012; Darnell et al., 2011; Maurin et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by ribosome profiling data analysis shown in Figure 7B and citations to CLIP-seq studies.

claim: There was a significant but weak correlation between the mislocalization and translational repression of transcripts due to FMRP.
source: We found a significant but weak correlation between the mislocalization (as measured by changes in LR) and translational repression (as measured by changes in ribosome occupancy) of transcripts due to FMRP (R = 0.08, p=4.1e-16).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of localization and ribosome profiling data.

claim: There was no significant overlap between the translational regulatory targets and the RNA localization targets of FMRP.
source: However, when we looked at the transcripts that were statistically significantly affected in the two conditions, we found no significant overlap between the translational regulatory targets and the RNA localization targets of FMRP, suggesting that the protein exerts these activities on largely distinct pools of transcripts (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of localization and translation target sets shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The localization targets of FMRP were enriched for genes that regulate transport in cells.
source: While the localization targets of FMRP were enriched for genes that regulate transport in cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 7), the translational regulatory targets were enriched for genes that regulate RNA metabolism and for those that regulate synaptic activity (Figure 7—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7.

claim: The translational regulatory targets of FMRP were enriched for genes that regulate RNA metabolism and for those that regulate synaptic activity.
source: While the localization targets of FMRP were enriched for genes that regulate transport in cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 7), the translational regulatory targets were enriched for genes that regulate RNA metabolism and for those that regulate synaptic activity (Figure 7—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 6.

claim: There was no relationship between the 3′ UTR G-quadruplex content of a transcript and whether or not it was translationally regulated by FMRP.
source: We also found no relationship between the 3′ UTR G-quadruplex content of a transcript and whether or not it was translationally regulated by FMRP (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Translational regulatory targets of FMRP were strongly enriched for having GC-poor, long CDS sequences.
source: Identifying transcript features associated with translational regulation by FMRP proved difficult as the transcript features most strongly associated with FMRP translation targets were the GC content and length of the transcript's CDS (Figure 7—figure supplements 7 and 8). Translational regulatory targets of FMRP were strongly enriched for having GC-poor, long CDS sequences.
evidence: This claim is supported by transcript feature analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplements 7 and 8.

claim: Transcripts that were more efficiently localized in the I304N sample contained significantly more G-quadruplexes than expected.
source: We found that transcripts that were more efficiently localized in the I304N sample contained significantly more G-quadruplexes than expected, indicating that the I304N mutant retains the ability to promote the localization of G-quadruplex-containing transcripts (Figure 7E, Supplementary file 1g).
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptome-wide sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Wildtype FMRP and the I304N mutant were transported to neurites with approximately equal efficiencies.
source: In support of this result, we found that wildtype FMRP and the I304N mutant were transported to neurites with approximately equal efficiencies, as had been previously reported (Figure 7—figure supplement 9; Schrier et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 9 and citations to previous studies.

claim: The I304N mutant was deficient in promoting the localization of G-quadruplex-containing messages compared to the wildtype when comparing localization data from cells expressing full length, wildtype FMRP to those expressing the I304N mutant.
source: When we compared localization data from cells expressing full length, wildtype FMRP to those expressing the I304N mutant, we found that the mutant was deficient in promoting the localization of G-quadruplex-containing messages compared to the wildtype (Figure 7—figure supplement 10, Supplementary file 1h).
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptome-wide sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 10.

claim: The I304N mutant is approximately four fold more lowly expressed than the wildtype in the rescue cells.
source: However, the I304N mutant is approximately four fold more lowly expressed than the wildtype in these cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 11).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 11.

claim: The decreased expression of the I304N mutant is consistent with previous reports of reduced I304N expression in I304N mouse mutants.
source: This decreased expression of the I304N mutant is consistent with previous reports of reduced I304N expression in I304N mouse mutants (Zang et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zang et al., 2009.

claim: The decrease in I304N protein expression is due to decreased protein stability.
source: Given that in our system the wildtype and I304N mutant proteins are integrated and expressed from the same locus using the same promoter, we propose that this decrease in I304N protein expression is due to decreased protein stability.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation and inference from the experimental setup.

claim: An FMRP mutant that is unable to regulate translation is still able to regulate the localization of G-quadruplex-containing transcripts.
source: From these results, we conclude that an FMRP mutant that is unable to regulate translation is still able to regulate the localization of G-quadruplex-containing transcripts.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the I304N mutant experiments.

claim: The recognition of a G-quadruplex sequence within the 3′ UTR of a transcript by the RGG domain of FMRP is associated with localization of the transcript.
source: We propose a model in which the recognition of a G-quadruplex sequence within the 3′ UTR of a transcript by the RGG domain of FMRP is associated with localization of the transcript.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the collective experimental data.

claim: The recognition of some as-yet unidentified transcript feature by one or both of the KH domains of FMRP may be associated with translational regulation.
source: Conversely, the recognition of some as-yet unidentified transcript feature by one or both of the KH domains of FMRP may be associated with translational regulation (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the experimental data.

claim: Some studies have found that the RGG domain of FMRP is required for efficient interaction of the protein with polyribosomes.
source: First, although some studies have found that the RGG domain of FMRP is required for efficient interaction of the protein with polyribosomes (Blackwell et al., 2010), other studies have found that the RGG domain of FMRP is at least partially dispensable for this interaction while the KH domains are absolutely required (Chen et al., 2014; Darnell et al., 2005b; Mazroui et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Blackwell et al., 2010.

claim: Other studies have found that the RGG domain of FMRP is at least partially dispensable for polyribosome interaction while the KH domains are absolutely required.
source: First, although some studies have found that the RGG domain of FMRP is required for efficient interaction of the protein with polyribosomes (Blackwell et al., 2010), other studies have found that the RGG domain of FMRP is at least partially dispensable for this interaction while the KH domains are absolutely required (Chen et al., 2014; Darnell et al., 2005b; Mazroui et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2014; Darnell et al., 2005b; and Mazroui et al., 2003.

claim: The I304N mutation abolishes polyribosome association.
source: Second, the I304N mutation, which is in one of the KH domains, abolishes polyribosome association (Feng et al., 1997) and translation repression activity (Laggerbauer et al., 2001), but not localization activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Feng et al., 1997.

claim: The I304N mutation abolishes translation repression activity.
source: Second, the I304N mutation, which is in one of the KH domains, abolishes polyribosome association (Feng et al., 1997) and translation repression activity (Laggerbauer et al., 2001), but not localization activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Laggerbauer et al., 2001.

claim: G-quadruplex sequences are unable to compete with polysomes for binding to FMRP.
source: Third, G-quadruplex sequences are unable to compete with polysomes for binding to FMRP (Darnell et al., 2005a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Darnell et al., 2005a.

claim: The dual functionalities of FMRP are driven by distinct binding capabilities of its different RNA binding domains.
source: Taken together, these findings support the idea that the dual functionalities of FMRP are driven by distinct binding capabilities of its different RNA binding domains.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on inference from multiple lines of evidence.

claim: Hundreds to thousands of transcripts are asymmetrically distributed within cells.
source: Hundreds to thousands of transcripts are asymmetrically distributed within cells, yet the mechanisms that regulate trafficking are known for only a handful (Cajigas et al., 2012; Gumy et al., 2011; Lécuyer et al., 2007; Taylor et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: FMRP has long been known to bind to G-quadruplex sequences.
source: FMRP has long been known to bind to G-quadruplex sequences (Anderson et al., 2016; Darnell et al., 2001; Suhl et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Anderson et al., 2016; Darnell et al., 2001; and Suhl et al., 2014.

claim: G-quadruplex sequences have been shown to be sufficient for transport to neurites.
source: FMRP has long been known to bind to G-quadruplex sequences (Anderson et al., 2016; Darnell et al., 2001; Suhl et al., 2014), and G-quadruplex sequences have been shown to be sufficient for transport to neurites (Subramanian et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Subramanian et al., 2011.

claim: The majority of RNA sequences that have the ability to fold into G-quadruplex structures in vitro may be generally unfolded in cells.
source: Recent reports have demonstrated that the majority of RNA sequences that have the ability to fold into G-quadruplex structures in vitro may be generally unfolded in cells (Guo and Bartel, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Guo and Bartel, 2016.

claim: G-quadruplex sequences have been reported to be under purifying selection.
source: Still, previous reports and our data demonstrate that the G-quadruplexes must be folded in order to be efficiently bound by FMRP (Subramanian et al., 2011), and G-quadruplex sequences have been reported to be under purifying selection (Lee et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2020.

claim: The I304N mutant, which is unable to inhibit translation but still able to regulate RNA localization, is associated with FXS phenotypes.
source: However, the fact that the I304N mutant, which is unable to inhibit translation but still able to regulate RNA localization, is associated with FXS phenotypes clearly points to the translational regulatory activity of FMRP being important.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the properties of the I304N mutant and its association with FXS.

claim: Loss of expression of the FMR1 gene in humans is associated with intellectual disabilities and occurs in approximately 1 in 5000 males.
source: Loss of expression of the FMR1 gene in humans is associated with intellectual disabilities and occurs in approximately 1 in 5000 males (Coffee et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Coffee et al., 2009 and represents established knowledge.

claim: FMRP-null mice display similar phenotypes to humans with Fragile X syndrome.
source: FMRP-null mice display similar phenotypes (Kazdoba et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kazdoba et al., 2014.

claim: FMRP has been shown to regulate RNA metabolism at the level of translational repression and RNA localization.
source: FMRP has been shown to regulate RNA metabolism at the level of translational repression and RNA localization (Darnell et al., 2011; Dictenberg et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Darnell et al., 2011 and Dictenberg et al., 2008.

claim: Genome-wide studies probing the translation repression activity of FMRP have been performed.
source: Although genome-wide studies probing the translation repression activity of FMRP have been performed (Darnell et al., 2011), much less is known about the RNAs that depend on FMRP for efficient localization to neuronal projections.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Darnell et al., 2011.

claim: FMRP has been implicated in the transport of a handful of RNAs.
source: FMRP has been implicated in the transport of a handful of RNAs (Dictenberg et al., 2008; Muddashetty et al., 2007; Zalfa et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dictenberg et al., 2008; Muddashetty et al., 2007; and Zalfa et al., 2007.

claim: Several studies have reported transcript and RNA motif targets for FMRP in vitro and in vivo.
source: Several studies have reported transcript and RNA motif targets for FMRP in vitro and in vivo (Ascano et al., 2012; Brown et al., 2001; Darnell et al., 2001, Darnell et al., 2005a; Vasilyev et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Considerable disagreement among studies remains about the identity of RNA sequences that interact with FMRP with high-affinity.
source: Several studies have reported transcript and RNA motif targets for FMRP in vitro and in vivo (Ascano et al., 2012; Brown et al., 2001; Darnell et al., 2001, Darnell et al., 2005a; Vasilyev et al., 2015), yet considerable disagreement among these studies remains about the identity of RNA sequences that interact with FMRP with high-affinity (Anderson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Anderson et al., 2016.

claim: RNA G-quadruplex sequences have been repeatedly identified as binding targets of FMRP.
source: RNA G-quadruplex sequences have been repeatedly identified as binding targets of FMRP (Blice-Baum and Mihailescu, 2014; Darnell et al., 2001; Schaeffer et al., 2001; Zhang et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Studies that have looked at commonalities between published datasets have found enrichments for WGGA sequences consistent with G-quadruplex formation.
source: RNA G-quadruplex sequences have been repeatedly identified as binding targets of FMRP (Blice-Baum and Mihailescu, 2014; Darnell et al., 2001; Schaeffer et al., 2001; Zhang et al., 2014), and studies that have looked at commonalities between published datasets have found enrichments for WGGA sequences consistent with G-quadruplex formation (Anderson et al., 2016; Suhl et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Anderson et al., 2016 and Suhl et al., 2014.
